sections.learningObjectives:
- Respond to a needlestick or sharps exposure by providing immediate first aid, reporting promptly, and following the facility's post-exposure procedure.
- Recognize the warning signs of syncope and respond by positioning the patient safely, protecting them from injury, and escalating to the provider.
- Apply scope-of-practice and supervision boundaries by performing only trained and authorized tasks and seeking guidance when unsure.
- Report exposures, incidents, abnormal results, and quality concerns accurately and promptly through the proper chain of command while protecting confidentiality.
- Document clinical events objectively and accurately, and correct any documentation errors through the approved method.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

If you poke yourself with a needle, the first thing to do is wash the spot right away with soap and warm water, like washing a cut. That helps rinse away any germs before they can get inside you.

### Question 2

After you wash the poke, you tell the grown-up in charge right away. You do not wait or hide it, because the sooner people know, the sooner they can help you.

### Question 3

If something splashes in your eye, you rinse it with clean water right away, just like washing dirt out of your eye at the sink.

### Question 4

Bloodborne germs are the ones that can hide in blood and make someone sick if the blood gets into a cut or a splash. The three big ones we protect against are hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV.

### Question 5

The exposure control plan is like a safety rulebook. It tells everyone at work which jobs could touch blood, and exactly what to do to stay safe and what to do if an accident happens.

### Question 6

An engineering control is a tool or machine that makes a job safer all by itself. A hard plastic box for used needles is a great example, because it catches the sharp point so nobody gets poked.

### Question 7

When you are done with a needle, you click the little safety cover over the point and drop it straight into the sharps box. You never try to bend it or leave it lying around.

### Question 8

Putting the cap back on a needle with both hands means you are pointing the sharp end at your own fingers. If you miss the cap, you poke yourself.

### Question 9

When the sharps box is full, you do not stuff more needles in. You close it and get a new box, so nobody has to push a hand down onto sharp points.

### Question 10

A sharps box has to be strong enough that needles cannot poke through it, sealed so liquid cannot leak out, and clearly marked so everyone knows not to reach inside.

### Question 11

An exposure means blood actually got inside your body through a break in the skin, like a cut. If it just touches healthy skin and you wash it off, the germs cannot get through.

### Question 12

Some body fluids, like blood or fluids with blood in them, can carry germs. But things like sweat and plain tears do not carry these germs, so they are treated differently.

### Question 13

We treat everyone's blood as if it could carry germs, because we cannot always tell who might be sick. That keeps both the patients and the workers safe.

### Question 14

Only a doctor or nurse gets to decide what medicine or treatment you need after a needle poke. Your job is to tell the grown-up in charge right away and follow instructions.

### Question 15

When something goes wrong, you write down exactly what happened, like the time and what needle was used. You write facts, not guesses or blame.

### Question 16

Some germs can make you sick much later without you feeling anything now. So even if you feel totally fine, you still tell someone about the poke right away.

### Question 17

You cannot just test someone's blood without asking them first. There are rules about getting permission, and you follow the office's rules instead of doing it yourself.

### Question 18

First wash with soap and water. You can put a little cleaning medicine on after, but never use harsh chemicals like bleach on your skin.

### Question 19

There is a shot that protects workers from hepatitis B, and the boss offers it so workers do not get sick if they are exposed to blood. It does not mean they can skip gloves.

### Question 20

If you are not sure something is a big deal, tell the person in charge anyway. It is better to say something and be told it is fine than to stay quiet and miss a real problem.

### Question 21

Instead of passing a sharp tool from hand to hand, you set it on a tray and let the other person pick it up. That way nobody gets poked in the middle of the handoff.

### Question 22

If glass breaks, you use a dustpan and brush to pick it up, never your fingers, and you put the sharp pieces in the special sharps box so nobody gets cut.

### Question 23

You throw the needle away right where you used it, so you do not have to carry a sharp point across the room where it could poke someone.

### Question 24

A work practice is a rule about how you act, like not eating or putting on lip balm near where blood is handled. It is about behavior, not equipment.

### Question 25

Even if you wore gloves, you still wash your hands when you take them off, because gloves can have tiny holes or your hands can get dirty while taking them off.

### Question 26

It can feel embarrassing to make a mistake, but you still tell the truth and fill out the paper, because keeping yourself safe is more important than feeling embarrassed.

### Question 27

Gloves help keep germs off your hands, but a needle can still poke right through them. They help, but they are not armor.

### Question 28

When you report a poke, the office can figure out what went wrong and fix it, so the same accident does not happen to someone else.

### Question 29

Your job after a poke is simple: wash it, tell the person in charge right away, and follow the office's plan. The doctors and nurses handle the medical part.

### Question 30

If something splashes into your mouth, you rinse with water and spit it out, then tell the person in charge. You do not swallow it or pretend it did not happen.

### Question 31

Syncope is the fancy word for fainting. It means the brain briefly does not get enough blood, so the person passes out for a short time.

### Question 32

Some people faint when they get scared or see blood, because their body overreacts and slows the heart and lowers blood pressure too fast, so the brain gets too little blood for a moment.

### Question 33

Before someone faints, they often feel dizzy or woozy, look pale, and start to sweat. These are warning signs that the brain is not getting enough blood.

### Question 34

If someone says they feel faint, you help them lie down or put their head down and call for help. You never tell them to stand up or leave them by themselves.

### Question 35

When you raise a fainted person's legs, it helps the blood flow back up to the brain, a little like tipping a bottle so the liquid runs where it is needed.

### Question 36

Right after someone faints, they are still sleepy and could choke if you give them food or a drink. You wait until they are fully awake and the provider says it is okay.

### Question 37

To stop someone from fainting during a blood draw, have them sit or lie down and remind them to speak up if they feel dizzy, so you can catch it early.

### Question 38

If someone starts to faint while standing, you help them sink down to the floor gently and shield their head, instead of trying to hold them up, which can hurt you both.

### Question 39

There is no one magic minute. You wait until the person is fully awake and the doctor or nurse says they are okay to go home.

### Question 40

After someone faints, you tell the doctor or nurse and write down what happened, even if the person seems fine afterward, so everyone has the record.

### Question 41

If someone who fainted does not wake up quickly, has trouble breathing, or has chest pain, you call for emergency help right away, because those are red flags.

### Question 42

Your job is to keep the person safe, help them lie down, and get the doctor or nurse. You do not figure out the cause or give medicine; the professionals do that.

### Question 43

Pale skin, sweating, and saying 'I'm going to pass out' are the body's alarm bell. You act right away to keep the person safe.

### Question 44

Smelling salts are not a normal thing to use when someone faints. You only use them if the doctor or the office rules say to, and you still get help.

### Question 45

If someone wakes up after fainting but seems confused, you keep them lying down, stay with them, and tell the doctor or nurse right away.

### Question 46

The safest spot for someone who feels faint is lying down flat, with their legs propped up a little, so blood can reach the brain.

### Question 47

If someone fainted, they should not just hop in the car. The doctor or nurse checks them first and decides if driving is safe.

### Question 48

If you are alone and someone faints, keep them safe and shout for help while staying right there with them. Do not run away and leave them.

### Question 49

A good sign after fainting is that the person wakes up quickly, is awake and alert, and can answer questions normally.

### Question 50

If someone has fainted before during a blood draw, you ask about it, have them lie down, and tell the nurse or doctor, so everyone is ready.

### Question 51

When someone is about to faint, you never leave them by themselves. You stay right there and help them lie down.

### Question 52

The vagus nerve is like a switch that, when triggered, tells the heart to slow down and the blood pressure to drop, which makes a person faint.

### Question 53

If someone who fainted is not waking up and is not breathing normally, that is an emergency. You call for emergency help right away and follow the office's emergency plan.

### Question 54

Asking if someone has fainted before helps you get ready, like having them lie down, so you can stop a faint before it happens.

### Question 55

If a patient goes quiet, turns pale, and their eyes roll up, they are fainting. You stop what you are doing, lay them down, and call for help.

### Question 56

Fainting is usually not serious and people wake up quickly, but you still keep them safe and tell the doctor or nurse, just in case.

### Question 57

If a patient faints during a draw, you stop, safely put the sharp away so nobody gets poked, and then take care of the patient.

### Question 58

Feeling dizzy when you stand up means your blood pressure dips when you change position. You help the person sit down and tell the doctor or nurse.

### Question 59

The best way to keep a fainting person safe is to have them lie down as soon as they feel dizzy, so they cannot fall and hurt themselves.

### Question 60

After someone faints, you let them rest lying down, then help them sit up slowly and stand up with help, so they do not get dizzy and faint again.

### Question 61

An assistant only does the jobs they have been trained and allowed to do, with a supervisor watching over them. They do not make big medical decisions on their own.

### Question 62

If someone asks you to do a job you have never learned, you say so and ask for help or training, instead of guessing and doing it wrong.

### Question 63

Some tests are simple and safe enough that a trained assistant can do them, but only after learning how and following the office's rules. They are not 'anything goes.'

### Question 64

If a test number looks wrong or unusual, you give it to the doctor or nurse and let them handle it. You never change it or explain it yourself.

### Question 65

Good note-taking means writing down exactly what happened, with real numbers, right away. You do not write guesses or leave things out.

### Question 66

Quality control is like checking that a scale reads zero before you use it. If the check fails, you stop, tell someone, and do not use the machine until it is fixed.

### Question 67

Labs need people who know what they are doing, because a well-trained worker does the test right and notices when something looks off.

### Question 68

When you are not sure what to do, you stop and ask the person in charge. It is always better to ask than to guess and make a mistake.

### Question 69

An assistant can label tubes, write down numbers, and tell the doctor about results, but they cannot be the one to decide what a result means or tell a patient their diagnosis.

### Question 70

Reporting through the chain of command means telling the right person in the right order, so the message lands where it can actually be fixed.

### Question 71

A near miss is when something almost went wrong but did not. You still tell someone, because finding out why it almost happened can stop it from happening for real.

### Question 72

If you make a mistake, you tell the truth right away so it can be fixed. Hiding it or blaming someone else makes things worse.

### Question 73

Drawing blood is a job you only do if you have been trained and a doctor or nurse is around, following the office's rules. You do not just do it on your own.

### Question 74

Writing down test results carefully and keeping them tidy means doctors can find the right information and trust that it is correct when caring for patients.

### Question 75

The assistant's part in lab quality is following the office's checklists and writing everything down correctly for every test, every time.

### Question 76

When something happens, you only tell the people who need to know to fix it and keep the patient safe. You do not gossip about it in the waiting room.

### Question 77

When you help a doctor during a procedure, you do exactly what they ask and only what you have been trained to do. You are the helper, not the one in charge.

### Question 78

If a patient starts to faint during a procedure, you speak up right away and help the doctor keep the patient safe.

### Question 79

Whether you can do a job depends on the rules: what the law says, what your office allows, whether you were trained, and whether the doctor gave the go-ahead.

### Question 80

If you are asked to do something you think you are not allowed to do, you speak up politely and ask about it, instead of just doing it or ignoring it.

### Question 81

The office rulebook is the safe way to do things. Even if a coworker shows you a faster shortcut, you follow the written rules because they are there to keep everyone safe.

### Question 82

A safe workplace is one where people feel okay telling about mistakes and problems, so they can be fixed, instead of being afraid to speak up.

### Question 83

If a patient asks what their test result means, you tell them the doctor or nurse will explain it. You do not try to explain medical results yourself.

### Question 84

Even if you learned a test somewhere else, in a new office you first read their steps and make sure you are officially checked off before doing it there.

### Question 85

Your job is to share information quickly and correctly and pass the big decisions to the doctors and nurses. You report, they decide.

### Question 86

The full correct response is: do the first aid you are trained to do, tell the doctor or nurse, write down what happened, and follow the office rules.

### Question 87

Learning does not stop after the first training. Workers keep practicing and getting checked so their skills stay sharp and patients stay safe.

### Question 88

If a machine is broken, you stop using it, put a sign on it, and tell someone. You do not keep using it or try to fix it yourself.

### Question 89

When you write about an accident, you write down the facts right away, without guessing or blaming anyone.

### Question 90

If you wrote something wrong, you fix it the official way: draw one line through it, write the correct thing, and sign and date it, so everyone can see what was changed and why.
